This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 15, treat 15.1.2 Understanding Iterator Categories as a design decision with costs and evidence. Input iterators support single-pass reading under their contracts. Forward iterators support multipass traversal. Bidirectional iterators add backward movement, random-access iterators add constant-time indexed movement, and contiguous iterators additionally describe contiguous element storage in C++20’s iterator model. These distinctions explain why std::distance can be constant time for a vector yet linear for a forward list. A binary-search algorithm can use logarithmic comparisons on a forward range while still performing substantial iterator movement. Complexity must count the relevant operations, not assume every increment or midpoint access has the same cost. slides.title: Trace consecutive removals
keyPoints: The starting vector contains one through six.
At the first position, one is erased and the returned iterator refers to two.
Two is kept, so the iterator advances to three.
Repeating this process produces two, four, and six.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 15, treat Trace consecutive removals as a design decision with costs and evidence. The starting vector contains one through six. At the first position, one is erased and the returned iterator refers to two. Two is kept, so the iterator advances to three. Repeating this process produces two, four, and six. The loop never caches an endpoint across erasure and never increments the returned iterator in the erase branch. A stronger manual trace includes two adjacent elements that both need removal. That exposes the common extra-increment defect immediately: after removing the first, the second shifts into its position and must be examined next. An alternating input alone can sometimes make a flawed traversal look plausible. slides.title: Evidence and interpretation
keyPoints: The erase loop leaves two, four, and six.
Saving index one identifies four before and after reserve because reserve does not reorder the sequence.
No iterator from the old allocation is used afterward.
Both containers report distance three, but the mechanisms differ: the vector supports random-access distance.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 15, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The erase loop leaves two, four, and six. Saving index one identifies four before and after reserve because reserve does not reorder the sequence. No iterator from the old allocation is used afterward. Both containers report distance three, but the mechanisms differ: the vector supports random-access distance, while the forward list requires traversal. Advancing the vector iterator by two reaches six. Equal returned values do not imply equal complexity. The loop’s two branches encode its invariant: the current iterator always identifies the next unclassified element or the current end. Erasing replaces that iterator with the operation’s valid successor. Keeping advances past the classified element. This reasoning scales better than trying to patch skipped values after a fragile loop has already run. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 15, treat Failure clinic — Reserve did not save the cached end as a design decision with costs and evidence. A program reserves enough vector capacity, caches end(), and appends while iterating. The author concludes that all iterators remain safe because storage did not move. The conclusion overlooks the changed end position. Revisit the operation-specific invalidation rules, and redesign the loop to process an explicit original count or stage new elements separately when that is the intended behavior. Another defect erases an element and then increments the invalid old iterator. Assign the returned iterator instead. A third defect saves an index across erasure before that index and later updates the wrong record. That is an identity error rather than necessarily a dangling-address error, so a memory sanitizer may not detect it.
